about: THE REALM OF THE DANES, 777-1076: who is king in any year, his wars, the raids that went out from the realm and the raids that fell on it, the laws and peaces a merchant lives under, the coin, and the church. Written 4 Oct 2026 for Design/content/realms. Every entry has its source (abbreviations as in chronicle_793.json: ARF = the Frankish royal annals, AB = the annals of Saint-Bertin, Ann. Fuld. = the annals of Fulda, Ann. Xant. = the annals of Xanten, ASC = the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; Adam = Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis, by book and chapter, written about 1075, so late for everything before 1000). (?) marks what could not be checked or what the sources leave in doubt. from/to are years; where the ends of a reign are not known the note says so and 'certainty' is 'uncertain'. 'where' in raids is a port id from ports_793.json when the place is a port of the game, a plain place name when it is not; 'place' always gives the plain name. Web searching was shut for this session, so the facts rest on the annals as the writer knows them and on the pages listed under 'sources'; chapter numbers of Adam, Thietmar and Rimbert should be checked against an edition before any is shown to a player.
sources: Annales regni Francorum (ARF), ed. Kurze, MGH SRG 6 (1895): years 777, 782, 798, 804, 808-815, 817, 819, 821-823, 825-828
Annales Fuldenses (Ann. Fuld.), ed. Kurze, MGH SRG 7 (1891): years 845, 850, 852, 854, 857, 873, 880-885, 891
Annales Xantenses (Ann. Xant.), MGH SRG 12: years 834-846, 864, 873; Annales Vedastini 879-886; Regino of Prüm, Chronicon 881-885

Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ed. Waitz, MGH SRG 55 (1884); English by C. H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921, public domain): chapters 7-8, 12-13, 16, 24, 31-32. Vita Rimberti (same volume), chapter 18
Einhard, Vita Karoli 14 and 17; Notker, Gesta Karoli ii.13 (both in A. J. Grant, Early Lives of Charlemagne, 1907, public domain)
Widukind of Corvey, Res gestae Saxonicae i.40, iii.65 (MGH SRG 60)
Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon i.17, iii.6, iii.24, iv.23-25 (MGH SRG NS 9)

Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum, ed. Schmeidler, MGH SRG 2 (1917): i.14-15, i.39, i.47-48, i.52, i.55, i.57-62, ii.3-4, ii.25-32, ii.39-40, ii.55-56, ii.77-79, iii.12-13, iii.18, iii.51, iii.54, iv.1-9

Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (ASC), manuscripts C, D, E: years 839 (=842), 851, 867, 991, 994, 1013-1019, 1023, 1025 (=1026), 1028, 1035, 1040, 1042, 1066, 1069-1070 (Giles 1847 and Ingram 1823 are public domain)
Encomium Emmae reginae (about 1041), books i-ii
Old English Orosius: the voyages of Ohthere and Wulfstan (about 890)
Ibrahim ibn Yaqub al-Turtushi on Hedeby (about 965), kept by al-Qazwini
Cnut's letter to the English of 1027 (in John of Worcester and William of Malmesbury)
Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum i.8-10 (Tiel and Utrecht, 1006-1007)
Diplomas of Otto I, no. 294 (26 June 965) and of Otto III, no. 41 (18 March 988), MGH DD
Capitularies: Herstal 779 c. 20, Thionville 805 c. 7 (MGH Capit. I nos. 20, 44); Pîtres 864 c. 25 (MGH Capit. II no. 273)
Runestones: Jelling DR 41 and DR 42; Hedeby DR 1 (Skarthi), DR 2 and DR 4 (Sigtrygg), DR 3 (Erik)
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla (about 1230; late, used only where marked uncertain); Saxo Grammaticus and Sven Aggesen (about 1185-1200; late)
Tree-ring dates: the Danevirke (737, 968), the north mound at Jelling (winter 958/959), Trelleborg (980/981), the Ravning bridge (about 980)
Coin study: B. Malmer, Nordiska mynt före år 1000 (1966), for the combination groups KG 3-12; C. Feveile on the Ribe coins; the Damhus hoard near Ribe, found 2018 (?)

Pages read to check dates, 4 Oct 2026: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Danish_monarchs ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horik_I ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horik_II ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigfred_and_Halfdan ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Olaf ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Bluetooth ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweyn_Forkbeard ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cnut ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_the_Good ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweyn_II_of_Denmark ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansgar ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danevirke ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedeby ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribe ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_coinage ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Diocese_of_Roskilde

rulers.name: Sigfred
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Not known. He is last named in 798; Godfred is first named in 804.
rulers.note: 777: the Saxon leader Widukind flees to him. 782: his envoy Halptani comes to Charles at the springs of the Lippe. 798: Charles's envoy Godescalc is killed on his way back from him. Nothing is said of the years 799-803.

rulers.name: Godfred
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.seat: not known; his fleet and horsemen gather at Sliesthorp in 804 and 808
rulers.how_ended: Murdered in the summer of 810 by one of his own retainers, with his fleet just home from Frisia. Notker says the killer was his own son, whose mother he had put away.
rulers.note: He may have been king before 804; that is only the first year he is named.

rulers.name: Hemming
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Died early in 812; the annals do not say how.
rulers.note: Godfred's brother's son. He made the peace of the Eider in 811.

rulers.name: Sigfred and Anulo
rulers.title: rival claimants
rulers.how_ended: Both killed in one battle in 812, with 10,940 men as the annals count them. Anulo's side won.
rulers.note: Sigfred was a nephew of Godfred; Anulo a nephew of an earlier King Harald.

rulers.name: Harald and Reginfrid
rulers.also: Harald Klak (a later byname), Heriold; Ragnfred
rulers.title: kings of the Danes, brothers
rulers.how_ended: Driven out in 813 by the sons of Godfred, who came back from exile among the Svear. Reginfrid was killed trying to return in 814.
rulers.note: Anulo's brothers. In 813 they were away with the army in Vestfold, 'the furthest part of their kingdom', when the sons of Godfred struck.

rulers.name: The sons of Godfred
rulers.also: four or five brothers; Horik is the only one named
rulers.title: kings of the Danes, ruling together
rulers.how_ended: The eldest was killed in 814; two were driven out in 819 when the other two took Harald back as a partner; from 827 Horik is the one king named.
rulers.note: In 815 they lay with 200 ships on an island three miles from the shore and would not fight the Frankish army.

rulers.name: Harald
rulers.title: king of the Danes, sharing the kingdom with two sons of Godfred
rulers.how_ended: Driven out of the partnership and out of the land in 827, a year after his baptism. He kept the county of Rüstringen in Frisia, the emperor's gift.
rulers.note: Put back in 819 by Obodrite ships on the emperor's order. A Harald, long among the Franks, was killed by the wardens of the Danish border in 852; it may be he (?).

rulers.name: Horik
rulers.also: Horic, Horik I, Horik the Old
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.seat: not known; he gives Anskar a plot for a church at Sliesthorp
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 854 in a three-day battle against his nephew Guthorm, who came home from raiding. Guthorm died too, and nearly all the royal kin.
rulers.note: A son of Godfred; one of the kings from 813, the only one named from 827. From 850 he shared the kingdom with two nephews who had made war on him.

rulers.name: Horik the Younger
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Not known. He is last named in 864, in a letter from Pope Nicholas I.
rulers.note: A boy of the royal kin, the one left alive in 854. In 857 he let Rorik hold the land between the sea and the Eider.
rulers.source: Ann. Fuld. 854, 857; Rimbert 31-32; letter of Nicholas I to Horik, 864 (MGH Epp. VI) (?)

rulers.name: No king is named
rulers.note: The sources are silent. Let people in the game say they do not know who is king, or name Horik still.

rulers.name: Sigfred and Halfdan
rulers.title: kings of the Danes, brothers
rulers.how_ended: Not known. They are named as kings only in 873. A King Sigfred and a King Godfred of the Northmen were killed on the Dyle in 891, and Adam of Bremen took them for kings of the Danes (?).
rulers.note: Only 873 is sure. The end year 891 is a guess, so that the game has an answer.

rulers.name: Helge
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Not known.
rulers.note: Known only from what King Svein Estridsson told Adam of Bremen about 1070: a king loved for his justice. The years are a guess.

rulers.name: Olaf
rulers.title: king among the Danes, come from the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Died; his sons Gnupa and Gurd had the kingdom after him.
rulers.note: Adam: he came from Sweden and took the Danish kingdom by force of arms. The years are a guess. His house may have held only the south, around Hedeby.

rulers.name: Gnupa and Gurd
rulers.title: kings at Hedeby, sons of Olaf
rulers.how_ended: Gnupa was beaten by King Henry of the East Franks in 934, made to pay tribute and baptised. What became of him is not known.
rulers.note: Gnupa in 934 is sure (Widukind). He is named on the two Hedeby stones his wife Asfrid, Odinkar's daughter, raised for their son. The start year is a guess.
rulers.source: Widukind i.40; Adam i.48; runestones DR 2, DR 4

rulers.name: Sigtrygg
rulers.title: king at Hedeby, son of Gnupa and Asfrid
rulers.how_ended: Deposed by Hardegon, son of Svein, who came from 'Nortmannia' (Norway, or Normandy (?)). His mother raised two stones for him at Hedeby.
rulers.note: The stones are sure; the years are not. Adam puts his fall twenty years earlier, under Archbishop Hoger (909-916), which does not fit Gnupa being king in 934.

rulers.name: Hardegon
rulers.title: king among the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Not known. Gorm, called his son, is king after him.
rulers.note: Overlaps the kings at Hedeby: the land may have been split, north and south, until about 936. Known only from Adam.

rulers.name: Gorm
rulers.also: Gorm the Old; Worm in Adam
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Died in the winter of 958/959 and was laid in the chamber of the north mound at Jelling; his son later moved him into the church (?).
rulers.note: His stone at Jelling for his wife Thyra has the oldest use of the name Denmark in the land itself. Adam calls him a savage enemy of Christians. The start year is not known.
rulers.source: Jelling stone DR 41; tree rings of the north mound's chamber, 958/959; Adam i.55, i.57, i.59

rulers.name: Harald Gormsson
rulers.title: king of the Danes, for a time of the Norwegians too
rulers.how_ended: Wounded in battle against his son Svein, he fled to Jumne at the Oder mouth and died there on All Saints' Day, in 985, 986 or 987.
rulers.note: Baptised about 963-965. His stone says he won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.
rulers.source: Jelling stone DR 42; Widukind iii.65; Thietmar iii.6; Adam ii.3, ii.25-28; Encomium Emmae i.1

rulers.name: Svein
rulers.title: king of the Danes; king of the English from Christmas 1013
rulers.how_ended: Died at Gainsborough on 3 February 1014, five weeks after England gave in to him.
rulers.note: Adam says the Svea king Erik drove him out and held Denmark for some years in the 990s; most now doubt it, since Svein was raiding England with a great fleet in 994 (?).
rulers.source: ASC (C/D/E) 994, 1003-1004, 1013, 1014; Adam ii.27-30, ii.39; Encomium Emmae i

rulers.name: Harald Sveinsson
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Died about 1018; nothing is told of how.
rulers.note: Svein's elder son, left to keep Denmark in 1013. He would not share the kingdom with Cnut but helped him fit out the fleet of 1015.

rulers.name: Cnut
rulers.title: king of the English, the Danes and the Norwegians
rulers.seat: Roskilde and Lund in Denmark; Winchester in England
rulers.how_ended: Died at Shaftesbury on 12 November 1035 and was buried at Winchester.
rulers.note: He came to Denmark to take the kingdom in the winter of 1019-1020. He was mostly in England: Thorkell (1023), then Earl Ulf (to 1026) kept Denmark, then his son Harthacnut as a boy king (?).

rulers.name: Harthacnut
rulers.title: king of the Danes; king of the English from 1040
rulers.how_ended: Died on 8 June 1042 at Lambeth, falling as he stood at his drink at a wedding feast.
rulers.note: He could not leave Denmark for five years for fear of Magnus of Norway, and lost England to his half-brother Harold until 1040.

rulers.name: Magnus
rulers.also: Magnus the Good, son of Olaf
rulers.title: king of the Norwegians and the Danes
rulers.seat: moving with his fleet; hailed at the Viborg thing (?)
rulers.how_ended: Died on 25 October 1047 in Denmark, on Zealand or aboard his ship (the tellings differ); he left Denmark to Svein and Norway to Harald.
rulers.note: He took Denmark by a treaty with Harthacnut that whoever lived longer should have both kingdoms (the sagas; about 1038-1040 (?)). Svein Estridsson, his earl in Jutland, rose against him from 1043.
rulers.source: Adam ii.77-79; ASC (D) 1047-1048; Heimskringla, Magnúss saga góða (late)

rulers.name: Svein Estridsson
rulers.title: king of the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Died on 28 April 1076 at Søderup in south Jutland (older books say 1074) and was buried at Roskilde. Five of his sons were kings after him.
rulers.note: Son of Earl Ulf and Estrid, Cnut's sister. He was Adam of Bremen's chief witness for the history of the north.

lords_abroad.name: Harald (Klak)
lords_abroad.holds: the county of Rüstringen, between the Jade and the Weser
lords_abroad.how_ended: Not known; perhaps the Harald killed on the Danish border in 852 (?).

lords_abroad.name: Harald the younger and his brother Rorik
lords_abroad.holds: Dorestad as a benefice in the last years of Louis the Pious; Walcheren and the places near it from 841
lords_abroad.how_ended: Harald died; Rorik was accused of treason about 844, was held, escaped and turned raider. Which Harald this is, is disputed (?).

lords_abroad.name: Rorik
lords_abroad.holds: Dorestad and the counties around it, later Kennemerland too
lords_abroad.under: Lothar I, Lothar II, then Charles the Bald and Louis the German
lords_abroad.how_ended: Last named in 873, when he swore to Louis the German at Aachen; dead by 882, when his lands went to Godfrid. The Frisians (the 'Cokingi') drove him out for a time in 867.

lords_abroad.name: Rodulf, son of Harald
lords_abroad.holds: nothing: a raider who demanded tribute of the Frisians of Oostergo
lords_abroad.how_ended: Killed in June 873 in Oostergo with 500 to 800 of his men (the annals differ), when the Frisians refused the tribute and fought.

lords_abroad.name: Godfrid
lords_abroad.holds: Frisia (Rorik's old lands), by the peace of Asselt, with the emperor's kinswoman Gisela as wife
lords_abroad.how_ended: Killed in June 885 at Herispich in the Betuwe, at a meeting with the emperor's men, after asking for wine lands on the Rhine. The last Danish lord in Frisia.

wars.who: Godfred against the emperor Charles: a stand-off, not a battle
wars.what: Charles carries off the Saxons beyond the Elbe and gives their land to the Obodrites. Godfred comes to Sliesthorp, on the border, with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom. He promises to meet the emperor and does not come; envoys go back and forth about the fugitives.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: One summer with an army in the market at Sliesthorp: fodder, ale and bread dear, Saxon fugitives living among the Danes, and a Frisian skipper asked whose man he is.

wars.who: Godfred, with the Wilzi, against the Obodrites and the Franks
wars.what: 808: Godfred storms Obodrite forts and makes two thirds of them pay tribute, losing his brother's son Reginold; he destroys Reric and builds his wall. 809: talks at Beidenfleth fail; Thrasco is murdered at Reric by Godfred's men. 810: the Franks fortify Esesfeld on the Stör; 200 ships fall on the Frisian islands; Godfred boasts he will come to Aachen and is murdered.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Reric is gone and its merchants and toll are at Sliesthorp. The land road between the two seas passes one gate. The Frisian coast pays 100 pounds of silver. The emperor orders a fleet and a coast watch. For a Frankish subject the Danish ports are enemy ports for three summers; 810 is also a year of cattle plague.

wars.who: The house of Harald against the house of Godfred
wars.what: Hemming dies. Sigfred and Anulo fight for the kingdom and both fall, with 10,940 men. Harald and Reginfrid rule a year, then the sons of Godfred come back from the Svear and drive them out. In 814 Reginfrid and Godfred's eldest son are killed, and Harald flees to the emperor.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nobody can promise a stranger safety: the king who took your toll in spring may be dead by autumn. The peace with the Franks holds on paper (sworn again in 813 by sixteen men a side), so the Eider crossing stays open.

wars.who: The emperor Louis's Saxons and Obodrites, for Harald, against the sons of Godfred
wars.what: 815: an army under the envoy Baldric crosses the Eider into Sinlendi and camps seven days on the shore; the sons of Godfred lie on an island with 200 ships and will not fight; the army burns, takes forty hostages and goes home. 817: the sons of Godfred, with the Obodrite Sclaomir, send a fleet up the Elbe against Esesfeld and are beaten off.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The country north of the Eider is plundered in 815. A Frankish hull at Sliesthorp or Ripa in these years is the enemy's.

wars.who: Harald and the sons of Godfred: a shared kingdom and its end
wars.what: 819: Harald is put back by Obodrite ships and shares the kingdom with two of Godfred's sons. Envoys go to the emperor almost every year (822, 823, 825, 826). 826: Harald is baptised at Mainz. 827: he is driven out. 828: at peace talks on the Eider he burns some Danish farms; the sons of Godfred cross the river, rout the Frankish camp, then send envoys to explain.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nine quiet years on the border: the best time before 873 for a Frisian at Sliesthorp, and the years the first Danish coins are struck. The scuffle of 828 is patched up within the year.

wars.who: Fleets from Denmark against Frisia and the Elbe; King Horik says they are not his
wars.what: 834-837: Dorestad is plundered four years running. 836 and 838: Horik's envoys tell the emperor he had no part in it and has caught and killed the leaders; in 838 he asks for Frisia and the Obodrites in return, and is laughed at. 845: Horik sends a great fleet (600 ships, the annals say) up the Elbe; Hamburg burns; the Saxons beat them; that autumn he sends to Louis at Paderborn offering peace, the captives and the loot. 847: Lothar, Louis and Charles together warn him to hold his people back or face war.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The home river of the house burns while the Danish ports are safe and full of Frisian cloth, Frisian silver and Frisian people for sale. A Frisian in Sliesthorp is tolerated, not loved, until the peace of 845.

wars.who: Horik against his nephews
wars.what: 850: two nephews make war on Horik and he buys peace by sharing the kingdom. 854: Guthorm, a nephew long away raiding, comes home with a fleet; in three days of fighting Horik, Guthorm and almost all the nobles die. One boy of the kin, Horik, is made king.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The men who knew the merchants are dead: Horik, who protected the church and the Christians at Sliesthorp, and his counsellors. The new count of the town shuts the church. It is the worst year to arrive with letters to the old king.

wars.who: Rorik and Godfrid, Danes in Frankish service, against Horik the Younger
wars.what: 855: Rorik and Godfrid, Harald's son, go home to try for the kingdom and fail. 857: Rorik takes a fleet to the border and, with King Horik's leave, holds the part of the kingdom between the sea and the Eider.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For a few years one lord takes the toll at Dorestad and at the Eider crossing (and perhaps at Sliesthorp (?)). While he is away in 857, other Danes sack Dorestad.

wars.who: The great army of Northmen in the Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt lands, under 'kings' Godfrid and Sigfred; not the Danish king's war, but Danes
wars.what: The army comes from England to Ghent in 879, winters at Nijmegen in 880-881, at Elsloo in 881-882, burns Cologne, Bonn, Aachen and Trier, is bought off at Asselt in 882 (Godfrid gets Frisia), burns Deventer, winters at Duisburg in 883-884, besieges Paris in 885-886 and is broken by King Arnulf on the Dyle in 891, where Sigfred and Godfred fall. In 892, after a famine, it crosses to England.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Every river port of the lower Rhine and Meuse burns at least once. Loot and captives come north to be sold. After 885 no Dane holds Frisia again; after 892 the Rhine is quiet for a hundred years.
wars.source: Ann. Fuld. 880-885, 891; Ann. Vedastini 879-892; Regino 881-885; ASC (A) 892

wars.who: Olaf from the land of the Svear and his sons, then Hardegon and Gorm
wars.what: About 900 a king Olaf comes from Sweden and takes the Danish kingdom by arms; his sons Gnupa and Gurd rule after him at Hedeby. About 936 Hardegon, son of Svein, comes from 'Nortmannia' and takes the kingdom from Gnupa's son Sigtrygg. All of this is Adam of Bremen, 170 years later, on King Svein's word; only Gnupa (934) and the stones for Sigtrygg are sure.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nothing is recorded. Hedeby goes on striking its thin pennies and the eastern silver goes on coming, so the town did not suffer much; a merchant deals with the king at Hedeby, not with a king of all the Danes.
wars.source: Adam i.48, i.52, i.55 (?); Widukind i.40; runestones DR 2, DR 4

wars.who: King Henry of the East Franks against the Danes of Gnupa
wars.what: Henry leads an army against the Danes, who had been raiding the Frisians by sea, beats them, makes them pay tribute and has King Gnupa baptised. Adam adds that he set the border at Schleswig, with a margrave and Saxon settlers (?).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The raids on Frisia from Hedeby stop. Hedeby pays tribute south for a time; Saxon merchants are at home there.
wars.source: Widukind i.40; Thietmar i.17; Adam i.57 (?)

wars.who: Harald Gormsson and Norway
wars.what: About 970 King Harald Greycloak of Norway is killed at Hals in the Limfjord; Earl Hákon rules Norway under the Danish king and pays tribute, then breaks away after 974. A Danish fleet with the Jomsborg men is beaten by Hákon at Hjörungavágr, about 986. Sagas only, so the years are loose.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For some years one king's peace covers the Skagerrak and the Vik: the road to Skiringssal's old waters is the Dane's.
wars.source: Jelling stone DR 42 ('won all Norway'); Heimskringla (late) (?)

wars.who: The emperor Otto II against Harald Gormsson
wars.what: After Otto I dies in 973 the Danes strike south. In 974 Otto II storms the wall at the gate called Wieglesdor, builds a fort on the border and leaves a garrison. In 983, while the emperor is beaten in Italy and the Slavs rise, the Danes take the fort by a trick, burn it and kill the garrison.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For nine years German soldiers sit beside Hedeby and the road south is the emperor's. The ring forts and the great bridge are built in these same years: the king is spending on timber, iron and men.

wars.who: Svein against his father Harald
wars.what: Svein rises with men who are tired of the old king's burdens. Harald is wounded, flees by ship to Jumne among the Slavs and dies. The year is 985, 986 or 987.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A short war. The ring forts are left to rot within a few years; the new king's men look west for silver.

wars.who: Danish fleets, then King Svein, then Cnut, against the English
wars.what: 991: Maldon and the first tribute. 994: Svein and Olaf at London. 1003-1005, 1006-1007: Svein's fleets ravage. 1009-1012: Thorkell's army. 1013: Svein takes the whole kingdom. 1015-1016: Cnut wins it again at Assandun.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: English silver pours into Denmark: 10,000 pounds in 991, 16,000 in 994, 24,000 in 1002, 36,000 in 1007, 48,000 in 1012, 82,500 in 1018. Every Danish port has men with pennies to spend and English goods to sell; an English port is a bad place to be a Dane in 1002.

wars.who: Erik, king of the Svear, against Svein (doubtful)
wars.what: Adam says Erik took Denmark and Svein was an exile for years, until Erik died. Svein's raids on England in these years make it unlikely as told; there may have been a Svea attack. The Hedeby stones for Skarthi and Erik, who died 'when warriors sat around Hedeby', may belong here, or to 983, or to about 1000.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: If it happened, Hedeby was besieged once in these years.
wars.source: Adam ii.30, ii.39 (?); runestones DR 1, DR 3

wars.who: Svein, Olof of the Svear and Earl Eirik against Olaf Tryggvason of Norway
wars.what: The sea fight at Svolder, 9 September 999 or 1000: Olaf is beaten and leaps overboard. Svein takes the Vik and the overlordship of Norway.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Danish king holds both shores of the Kattegat and the mouth of the Vik until 1015.

wars.who: Cnut makes Denmark his
wars.what: Cnut winters in Denmark in 1019-1020 after his brother's death and writes home that he has dealt with the danger that threatened from there. In 1022 he 'went out with his ships to Wiht', which may be the Isle of Wight or Witland east of the Vistula (?). In 1023 he is reconciled with Thorkell and leaves him Denmark and his son.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: From 1019 one king rules from Lund to London. English moneyers, bishops and cloth come east; the first regular Danish coinage begins.

wars.who: Cnut against Olaf of Norway and Anund of the Svear, and against his own earl Ulf
wars.what: 1026: Ulf and Eilaf come against Cnut with a fleet and army from Sweden at the Holy River; many of Cnut's men, Danes and English, die and the Swedes hold the field, but Cnut keeps Denmark. Earl Ulf is killed in the church at Roskilde that Christmas (late sources). 1028: Cnut takes Norway with fifty ships and English silver. 1030: Olaf is killed at Stiklestad.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Holy River is by Áhús (if it is the river in Skåne and not one in Uppland (?)): stay out of Skåne's waters in 1026. After 1028 Cnut's peace runs from the Vik to the Thames.

wars.who: Magnus of Norway against Harthacnut
wars.what: The Norwegians throw out Cnut's son Svein in 1035 and take Magnus as king. He threatens Denmark until the two kings meet at the Göta river and swear that the longer-lived shall have both kingdoms (sagas).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Harthacnut cannot leave Denmark for five years; the fleet is kept at home and the coasts watched.

wars.who: Magnus against Svein Estridsson, and against the Wends
wars.what: 1042: Magnus takes Denmark and makes Svein his earl. 1043: Svein claims the kingdom; Magnus burns Jumne at the Oder mouth; a great Wendish army ravages Jutland as far as Ripa and is destroyed on Lyrskov heath by Hedeby on 28 September. 1044-1045: Magnus beats Svein at sea several times (Aarhus, Helgenæs). 1047: Magnus dies and names Svein his heir in Denmark.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: South Jutland is overrun in 1043. The Oder market at Jumne is burnt. Which king a port holds with changes more than once; a ship is asked whose man her master is.
wars.source: Adam ii.77-79; Heimskringla, Magnúss saga góða (late)

wars.who: Harald Sigurdsson of Norway against Svein Estridsson
wars.what: Almost every summer Harald's fleet burns along the Danish coasts. About 1049-1050 he burns Hedeby from end to end, and Aarhus (?). 9 August 1062: he wins the sea fight at the Nissan river in Halland, and Svein escapes ashore. 1064: the kings make peace at the Göta river, each keeping his own.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Sixteen bad summers for the open coasts of Jutland, Funen and the Belts. Hedeby does not recover: its trade moves across the water to Schleswig. Roskilde and Lund, away from the Norwegian's reach, grow.
wars.source: Adam iii.12-13 (?); Heimskringla, Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar (late), with the skalds' verses

wars.who: The heathen Obodrites and Lutici against their Christian prince and his neighbours
wars.what: Prince Gottschalk, King Svein's son-in-law, is killed at Lenzen on 7 June 1066. The rising burns Hamburg and falls without warning on Schleswig, 'very rich and full of people', and destroys it.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The end of the old port at the head of the Schlei, in the last year of the game.

wars.who: Svein Estridsson against William of England
wars.what: A Danish fleet under the king's brother Asbjörn joins the English rebels, takes York in September 1069, winters in the Humber, plunders Peterborough from Ely in 1070 and goes home when William pays.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: After the end of the game. The last time a Danish king's fleet takes an English town.

raids.what: He destroys the Obodrites' trading place, which had paid him a good toll, puts its merchants aboard his ships and sets them down at Sliesthorp.

raids.place: the islands off the Frisian coast, and the mainland
raids.who: a fleet of 200 ships from the land of the Northmen, sent by Godfred
raids.what: All the islands are laid waste; the Frisians lose three fights on the mainland and have paid 100 pounds of silver in tribute by the time the news reaches the emperor.

raids.place: the Frankish fort north of the Elbe
raids.who: the sons of Godfred, with the Obodrite Sclaomir
raids.what: A fleet comes up the Elbe and wastes the banks of the Stör while Gluomi, the warden of the Danish border, comes by land; the garrison holds.

raids.where: Flanders, the Seine mouth, Bouin in Aquitaine
raids.who: thirteen pirate ships from the land of the Northmen
raids.what: Beaten off in Flanders and at the Seine by the coast guard, they plunder Bouin and go home with great booty.
They lay waste part of Frisia, come by Utrecht to Dorestad and plunder everything; some people are killed, some carried off, part of the town burnt.
They fall on Dorestad a second time and waste it. The emperor orders the coast defended.
They burn Antwerp, and Witla at the mouth of the Maas, and take tribute from the Frisians. Horik's envoys say the king had no hand in it.
The trading place is burnt and is not heard of again.
Dorestad and Frisia are wasted a third time.
On 17 June they surprise Walcheren, kill Count Eggihard and the Dane Hemming, Halfdan's son, who fought for the emperor, carry off many women, then go on to Dorestad and take tribute there too.
They come up the Seine in May, burn Rouen and the abbey of Jumièges and take ransom from Saint-Wandrille.
They fall on the port at dawn, plunder, kill and carry off, and leave only the houses that paid. The same summer there is great slaughter at London and Rochester, and Hamwic is raided.

raids.who: King Horik's fleet (600 ships, the annals say)
raids.what: The town is surrounded in an evening and taken; church, cloister and Anskar's books burn in a day and two nights; Anskar gets away with the relics. The Saxons then beat the fleet. In the autumn Horik offers peace and to give back captives and loot.

They come up the Seine in March, enter Paris at Easter and take 7,000 pounds of silver to go. A sickness kills many of them on the way home; at Horik's court the envoy of Louis hears the king order the rest seized (?).
raids.source: AB 845; Ann. Xant. 845; Translatio S. Germani

raids.what: They take tribute from Frisia as they please and burn Dorestad and two other places while Lothar looks on from Nijmegen. In 847 Danes hold Dorestad and the Betuwe.
He comes with a fleet from the Danes, takes Dorestad and holds it; Lothar, unable to drive him out, grants it to him for his oath and his promise to keep other Danes away.
They storm Canterbury and London and put the Mercian king to flight, then are beaten at Aclea by Æthelwulf of Wessex.

raids.who: Danes, while Rorik is away in Denmark
raids.what: They break into Dorestad and plunder the whole island of the Batavians and the places near it.

In January they come up the Rhine, sack Dorestad and a large settlement where the Frisians had fled, kill many Frisian merchants and take many people, and go on to an island by Neuss. The last sack: the town is not named as a port again.
They take York on All Saints' Day; in March 867 both Northumbrian kings die trying to take it back.

He demands tribute of the Frisians of Oostergo; they answer that they owe it to none but King Louis, fight, and kill him and hundreds of his men. A Northman long baptised and living among them advises the Frisians how to end it.

raids.who: the great army, come from England
raids.what: It winters in the abbey of Saint Bavo at Ghent and wastes Flanders and Brabant from there.
It winters in the king's palace at Nijmegen, is besieged there by Louis the Younger, and burns the palace when it leaves early in 881.

raids.place: Cologne, Bonn, Aachen and the Meuse towns
raids.who: the great army under Godfrid and Sigfred, from its camp at Elsloo
raids.what: Liège, Maastricht, Tongeren, Cologne, Bonn, Zülpich, Jülich and Neuss burn; horses are stabled in the palace chapel at Aachen; Prüm and Trier follow at Epiphany and Easter 882.

raids.who: Northmen, after the peace of Asselt
raids.what: They burn the port of Deventer, where Saint Lebuin lies, and kill many.
They seize Duisburg, build a fort and winter there, hemmed in by Duke Henry; in spring 884 they burn the camp and go.

raids.who: the great army under Sigfred and others
raids.what: The siege of Paris, from November 885 to the autumn of 886; the emperor buys them off with 700 pounds and leave to go up to Burgundy.
raids.source: Abbo, Bella Parisiacae urbis; Ann. Vedastini 885, 886

raids.who: a fleet of 93 ships under Olaf (Tryggvason); King Svein may have been with it (?)
raids.what: Folkestone, Sandwich and Ipswich are overrun; Ealdorman Byrhtnoth falls at Maldon; 10,000 pounds are paid.

raids.who: Olaf and King Svein with 94 ships
raids.what: On 8 September they try to burn the town and are beaten off with more loss than they looked for; they ravage the south and are paid 16,000 pounds.

raids.place: Stade and the Elbe and Weser mouths
raids.who: sea raiders, Danes and Svear by Adam's account
raids.what: On 23 June they beat the Saxon counts, take several noble prisoners, and when one escapes cut off the hands, ears and noses of the hostages; the ransoms empty the country of silver.

raids.who: not known: the besiegers are 'drengs'; two of the dead were King Svein's men
raids.what: Two stones by Hedeby remember men who died 'when the drengs sat around Hedeby': Skarthi, King Svein's retainer, who had been in the west, and Erik, a steersman, whose partner (félagi) Thorulf raised his stone. The year is a guess between 983 and about 1000.

In 1006 they come up the Waal and burn Tiel. In 1007 they come up the Lek to Utrecht; the townsmen burn their own harbour quarter so that it cannot be used against the walls, and the raiders spare the churches and go.
raids.source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum i.8-10

raids.what: London holds out against him in the autumn, with King Æthelred and Thorkell inside; when all the rest of England has given in, the townsmen give hostages too.
His ships come to Greenwich in May; he digs a channel round the south end of the bridge, drags the ships through and rings the town with a ditch, so that no one can go in or out. London holds.

raids.who: King Magnus with a Danish and Norwegian fleet
raids.what: He besieges and burns the richest Slav market on the Baltic.
raids.source: Adam ii.79 and scholion (?); Heimskringla, Magnúss saga góða (late)

raids.what: It ravages north through Jutland as far as Ripa; Magnus meets it on the heath by Hedeby on 28 September, on its way home, and cuts it down (15,000 dead, Adam says).
He burns the town from end to end; his skalds boast of the fire seen from the rampart before dawn. The wrecks in the harbour mud are from this time. The year is 1049 or 1050.
raids.source: Heimskringla, Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar 34 (late; the verses are of the time); Adam iii.13 (?)

raids.who: the heathen Wends, after the killing of Prince Gottschalk
raids.what: They fall on the town without warning and destroy it. What is left of its people and trade is on the north shore, at Schleswig.

raids.who: King Svein's fleet under his brother Asbjörn, with the English rebels
raids.what: They storm the two castles at York on 21 September and kill the Norman garrison. After the end of the game.

laws.what: Frankish law, in force all through the first age of the game: no mail coat may be sold outside the realm (Herstal, 779); none may be given to a merchant (803); trade over the eastern border goes only by the named border posts, and no arms pass there (Thionville, 805).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The thing a Dane pays most for is the thing the emperor forbids you to carry. The law names the Slav border, not the Danish one, but a count at Dorestad reads it as he likes.
laws.source: MGH Capit. I no. 20 c. 20; no. 40 c. 7 (?); no. 44 c. 7

laws.what: Godfred moves the merchants of Reric to Sliesthorp. The toll they paid him at Reric they now pay at his own port.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: From 809 the market for Baltic goods nearest the west is Sliesthorp, and the toll there is the Danish king's. A Reric man you knew is now there, not by his own choice.

laws.what: Godfred orders the border toward Saxony shut with a rampart from the eastern sea to the western, with one gate for wagons and horsemen.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Everything going by land between the Danes and the south passes one gate, where it can be counted, taxed or turned back. (The spade shows the great wall was already old: a main phase is dated to 737 by its timbers. Godfred repaired or added; the game should not call the wall new.)
laws.source: ARF 808; tree-ring dates of the Danevirke

laws.what: The peace of the Eider: twelve chief men of the Franks and twelve of the Danes swear peace on the river, each by his own custom. It is sworn again in 813 by sixteen a side, and confirmed in 825.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The Eider is the border: south of it the emperor's count answers for you, north of it the Danish king. While the oath holds a Frisian ship may lie at Ripa and Sliesthorp as a guest, not an enemy.

laws.what: Harald, baptised, is given the county of Rüstringen as a refuge, and takes the priests Anskar and Autbert north with him. Anskar buys boys to teach.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Danish lord, the emperor's man, holds the mouth of the Weser. A priest is to be found on the Danish border, and he buys captive boys.

laws.what: King Horik lets Anskar build a church at Sliesthorp, 'the port of his kingdom where merchants come together from every side', gives the plot, and lets anyone in his kingdom become Christian. (About 849-852.)
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Rimbert says it outright: after this the merchants of Dorestad and of Hamburg came there freely and without fear, which had not been so before, and goods of every kind were plentiful. A Christian can hear Mass and be buried at Sliesthorp.

laws.what: After the slaughter of 854 Hovi, the count of the port of Sliesthorp, shuts the church and forbids the Christian rite. Within a year or two the young king puts him out, lets the church open again, allows it a bell, a thing the heathen had held to be an abomination (Rimbert's word is nefandum), and gives a plot for a second church at Ripa. (About 855-860.)
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The port has a count of its own, and he is the man who can shut a church or a quay. The bell is the sign of how things stand: when it rings, Christians trade openly.

laws.what: West Frankish law, the edict of Pîtres: whoever sells or gives a mail coat, arms or a horse to the Northmen dies as a traitor.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: On Charles the Bald's rivers the old trade in swords is now a hanging matter, with no ransom.

laws.what: Envoys of King Sigfred come to Louis the German after Easter to make peace on the border between Danes and Saxons, 'and so that merchants of either kingdom, crossing to the other and bringing their wares, might buy and sell in peace'; the king agrees. In August the envoys of Sigfred's brother Halfdan bring a sword with a golden hilt, ask the king to hold the brothers as sons, and swear the peace on their weapons.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The first merchants' peace of the north in writing. A Saxon or Frisian may carry goods over the Eider and a Dane may come south, and each king answers for the other's traders.

laws.what: Not a law, a statement of it: Ohthere tells King Alfred that the port 'at the Heaths' lies between the Wends, the Saxons and Angeln 'and belongs to the Danes'; Wulfstan sails from it to Truso in seven days and nights.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Whoever rules, the toll at Hedeby is the Danish king's, and it is the place to find a ship for the east.

laws.what: The Danes at Hedeby are made tributary to King Henry, and their king Gnupa is baptised. Adam adds a margrave and a settlement of Saxons at Schleswig (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For a time tribute goes south from Hedeby and Saxon traders have their king's weight behind them there. The sea raids on Frisia that caused the war stop.

laws.what: Otto I frees the lands of the churches of Schleswig, Ripa and Aarhus 'in the march or kingdom of the Danes' from every due and service to the emperor (26 June 965). Otto III repeats it in 988, adding Odense and letting the bishops buy land.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The emperor claims a right over the Danish towns, if only on parchment, and gives it away to the bishops. A bishop's steward is a buyer of wine, wax, glass, cloth and books in each of these towns.
laws.source: MGH DD Otto I no. 294; DD Otto III no. 41

laws.what: King Harald, baptised, orders his people to hold to Christ alone and to honour his priests. (About 963-965.)
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: In the king's towns Sunday, the Friday fast and Lent begin to count, and fish sells better for it. In the country little changes for a generation: a traveller at Hedeby about this time found few Christians and one church.
laws.source: Widukind iii.65; Jelling stone DR 42; al-Turtushi

laws.what: After Otto II's victory an imperial fort stands on the border by Hedeby with a garrison, until the Danes burn it in 983.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For nine years the road south from Hedeby is watched by the emperor's men, and a toll is likely taken twice (?).

laws.what: King Harald's works: ring forts of one plan at Trelleborg, Fyrkat, Aggersborg, Nonnebakken and Borgring, and a timber bridge 760 m long over the Vejle valley at Ravning. All are built about 975-981 and let fall within twenty years.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The king can call up timber, iron, food and labour from the whole land, and for a few years he buys heavily. The bridge carries carts dry-shod on the army road north.

laws.what: Cnut's order in England (the Oxford meeting of 1018: 'Edgar's law') and his coinage carried to Denmark: pennies of the king's type struck by named moneyers in the king's towns.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: In Lund, Roskilde, Viborg and Ripa silver begins to pass by count, not only by weight, and a moneyer changes foreign coin for the king's at a charge. In the country the scale stays in the purse.

laws.what: The emperor Conrad II makes friendship with Cnut and gives up the march beyond the Eider with the town of Schleswig; the bond is sealed by betrothing Cnut's daughter Gunhild to Conrad's son Henry (married 1036). The year of the grant is put between 1025 and 1035.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The Eider is the border again, as in 811, and stays so. Hedeby and Schleswig are the Danish king's without dispute.

laws.what: Cnut at Rome, at the emperor's crowning (Easter, 26 March), complains to the emperor, King Rudolf of Burgundy and the other princes of the barriers and unjust tolls on the roads to Rome. They grant that all his men, English and Danes, 'merchants as well as those who travel for the sake of prayer', shall go and come in firm peace without barrier or toll-taker.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The first time a king of the north bargains for his merchants abroad. A Dane or Englishman on the Rhine road and the Alpine passes may plead the king's letter against a toll.
laws.source: Cnut's letter of 1027 (John of Worcester; William of Malmesbury)

laws.what: The law of the king's household men (Vederlov): a man of Cnut's guard answers for a wrong only before the king and his fellows. Known only from Sven Aggesen and Saxo, about 1185-1200, who give it to Cnut (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A quarrel with one of the king's men cannot be taken to the town's own court. Settle it, or leave.

laws.what: King Svein and Archbishop Adalbert divide Denmark into bishoprics: Schleswig, Ripa, Aarhus, Viborg and Vendsyssel in Jutland, Odense on Funen, Roskilde on Zealand, Lund and Dalby in Skåne. (About 1060.)
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Each chief town now has a bishop, a church with a school, feast-day markets and a household that buys. There is no tithe yet.

laws.what: Not a law but the custom Adam describes about 1070: the sea raiders of Zealand pay the king a tribute for leave to plunder the heathen around the Baltic, and often turn on their own people; a captive is sold without pity, friend or stranger.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A pirate in the Belts may be a taxpayer of the king you paid toll to. A ransom is a trade like another. Adam also gives the sailings: from Schleswig to the Slavs, the Svear and Samland; from Ripa to Frisia, England and Saxony; from Aarhus to the islands, Skåne and Norway.

coins.what: The small thick silver pieces of Ripa, with a staring face on one side and a backward-looking beast on the other (the 'Wodan and monster' sceattas), about 1 g. They are lost one by one in the market layers at Ripa, so they were used there by count.
coins.note: Old coin in 793 but still in purses. Outside Ripa it is silver by weight.

coins.what: Silver by weight: Arab dirhams from the east by way of Birka, Gotland and the Wends, rings, bars and cut pieces, tested by nicking and weighed on a folding balance against lead and iron weights.
coins.note: The ordinary money of the Danes for the whole first half of the game. Dirhams grow rare after about 970.

coins.what: The first coins made under the Danish kings: thin pennies copying Charlemagne's Dorestad penny and the old Ripa pieces, with ships, a stag, faces, houses, snakes and cocks (Malmer's groups KG 3-6).
mints: Ripa (the Damhus hoard of 2018 points to Ripa for the face and stag type (?))
coins.note: A Dorestad man would know his own town's name, badly copied, on a Danish coin. No king's name is on them.

coins.what: Hedeby's thin light pennies (KG 7-9), a worn-out copy of the CAROLVS and DORSTAD penny, some so thin the stamp shows through. Taken by count in the town and near it; elsewhere weighed.
coins.note: Dorestad has been gone forty years and more when these are struck; its name outlives it on Danish silver.

coins.what: King Harald's cross pennies (KG 10-12): thin, with a cross, made in Jutland in the years of the ring forts and found at them.
coins.note: No king's name. Likely made to pay the king's men.
coins.source: Malmer 1966; finds at the ring forts (?)

coins.what: Foreign pennies in great numbers: English (Æthelred's and Cnut's, from the tributes) and German (the Otto and Adelheid pennies of the Harz silver, Cologne, Frisian). Used by weight, nicked to test.
coins.note: Hoards of these years hold more English pennies than have been found in England.

coins.what: The first coin with a Danish king's name: ZVEN REX AD DENER, copied from Æthelred's penny with the cross and CRVX, by the moneyer Godwine. Eight are known.
mints: not named on the coin; Lund or Roskilde (?)
coins.note: A small issue, a king showing he could. Olaf in Norway and Olof at Sigtuna did the same in the same years, with the same English moneyer's name (?).

coins.what: Cnut's Danish pennies: the first regular coinage, on the English pattern, with the king's name, the moneyer's and the town's. Many moneyers have English names.
coins.note: Weights differ between east and west Denmark. English and German pennies still pass by weight beside them.

coins.what: Harthacnut's and Magnus's pennies: the same towns and more (Aarhus, Aalborg), with local designs; under Magnus the first copies of Byzantine coins appear.
coins.note: The Byzantine patterns come home with the men who served in the emperor's guard.

coins.what: Svein Estridsson's pennies: many types, several copied from Byzantine gold and silver (Christ enthroned, an emperor and an angel), and from about 1065 pennies of Lund with the moneyer's name in runes.
coins.note: The king's coin slowly drives out weighed silver in the towns. Only after 1074, under his son Harald, is foreign coin shut out.

church.what: Ebo, archbishop of Reims, with the pope's leave and the emperor's, preaches among the Danes for a summer and baptises many.

Harald is baptised with his wife and more than 400 followers (the number is from the annals of Xanten (?)) at Saint Alban's by Mainz, with the emperor as godfather. The monks Anskar and Autbert go north with him and begin a school with twelve bought boys.
church.source: ARF 826; Ann. Xant. 826 (?); Ermold, In honorem Hludowici iv; Rimbert 7-8

church.what: Anskar leaves the Danes for Birka; Autbert has gone home sick and dies. The mission among the Danes lapses after Harald's fall.
Hamburg is made the see for the north, with Anskar as archbishop and the pope's legate to the Danes, Svear and Slavs. (The founding papers were altered later; some put it in 834.)
Hamburg is burnt by Horik's fleet. Anskar is given Bremen as well (848); the two sees are joined, confirmed by Pope Nicholas I in 864.
The first church among the Danes is built at Sliesthorp, dedicated to Saint Mary (?), with a priest. (About 849-852.)
The church at Sliesthorp is shut by the count Hovi and its priest driven out; then opened again by the young King Horik, with a bell. (About 855-857.)
A church is built at Ripa on a plot the king gives, with leave for a priest to live there. Graves by the later cathedral go back to these years.
Pope Nicholas I writes to King Horik, thanks him for his gifts and urges him to leave idols and be baptised.
church.source: letter of Nicholas I (MGH Epp. VI) (?)

church.what: Anskar dies at Bremen on 3 February. Rimbert, his pupil, is archbishop to 888 and still visits the Danes: at Sliesthorp he gives his horse and saddle to free a captive nun he hears singing psalms in a chain of slaves.

King Gnupa is baptised on Henry's order. Thietmar says Henry also ended the great sacrifice at Lejre, the chief place of the kingdom, held every nine years in January, with ninety-nine men and as many horses, dogs and cocks; he wrote eighty years later.

Archbishop Unni of Hamburg-Bremen comes to the Danes. King Gorm will not hear him; his son Harald lets him preach and lets priests into the churches. Unni sails on to Birka and dies there on 17 September 936.
Three bishops for the Danes sit at the synod of Ingelheim on 7 June: Hored of Schleswig, Liafdag of Ripa, Reginbrand of Aarhus. Whether they ever lived in their towns is not known.
church.source: acts of the synod of Ingelheim (MGH Const. I); Adam ii.4

church.what: The priest Poppo carries a glowing iron in his hand before King Harald and shows it unburnt; the king is baptised. He raises the great stone at Jelling with Christ on it, builds a wooden church between his father's mounds and moves Gorm's bones into it (?). (About 963-965.)
church.source: Widukind iii.65; Jelling stone DR 42; excavations at Jelling

church.what: A bishop of Odense is named for the first time, with those of Schleswig, Ripa and Aarhus, in Otto III's charter.

Adam says King Svein threw out the bishops and went back to the old gods until God punished him. It is likelier that he only shut out the German bishops: he had churches built at Roskilde and Lund and brought bishops from England (Gotebald, for Skåne).
church.source: Adam ii.27-30, ii.41 (doubtful); Encomium Emmae i

church.what: Cnut has three bishops for Denmark hallowed by Archbishop Æthelnoth of Canterbury: Gerbrand for Roskilde, Bernhard for Skåne, Reginbert for Funen. Archbishop Unwan of Hamburg-Bremen seizes Gerbrand on his way and makes him swear obedience; Cnut gives way.
Cnut is at Rome for the emperor's crowning, prays at the apostles' tombs and wins lower charges for his archbishops' palls as well as the freedom of the roads.
Estrid, Cnut's sister, builds the first stone church in Denmark at Roskilde, where her husband Earl Ulf was killed in the wooden one at Christmas 1026 (late tellings).
Adalbert becomes archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen (to 1072) and means to be patriarch of the whole north. At Lyrskov the Danes and Norwegians say Saint Olaf rode with them.
Adalbert forces King Svein to put away his wife Gunhild, his kinswoman, under threat of the ban; then the two feast for eight days at Schleswig and are allies. (About 1050-1053.)
Denmark is divided into nine bishoprics; William, an Englishman who was Cnut's clerk (?), is bishop of Roskilde. Adam counts 300 churches in Skåne, 150 on Zealand and 100 on Funen.
The heathen rising among the Wends kills Prince Gottschalk (7 June), stones the monk Ansver and his brothers, and kills Bishop John of Mecklenburg (10 November); Schleswig is destroyed.
Adam of Bremen comes to King Svein, who 'held all the deeds of the barbarians in his memory as if they were written', and takes down from him much of what is known of the Danish kings before 1000.
